newsitem.title: UK: Stay long dlr/Frf on French policy angst -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Stay long dlr/Frf on French policy angst -analysts.

text.p: As French political angst about existing exchange rate policy intensifies, analysts said the best way to position for any concession to internal dissent is to buy dollars, not necessarily marks, for French francs.
Rumblings of discontent about the strength of the franc, especially against the dollar, have emanated from the French political sidelines in recent weeks and have grown in volume.

Comments from politicians such as former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing to Bank of France policy maker Paul Marchelli threaten to undermine confidence in France's long-standing "franc fort' policy, which has survived 10 years of both socialist and conservative administrations.

But analysts noted the sensitive mark/franc rate has held stable amid this unusually public policy debate. Optimism about the French government's committment to a punctual start for European monetary union in 1999 was most likely overriding policy jitters on that rate for now, they said.

Despite the remarkable resilience of the mark/franc cross, however, analysts said long dollar/French franc positions look "The sudden heightening of the debate about franc fort is more symptomatic of a battle within Europe, particularly between Germany and France, for the heart and soul of the future euro," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "Being long dollar/Paris is the best way to expoit these tensions."
Meggyesi said franc fort dissenters were mostly concerned with the relative strength of the future European single currency, or euro, against the dollar after the start of monetary union.

Since Giscard d'Estaing kicked off this debate on November 20 by calling for franc depreciation, dollar/franc has surged 2.8 percent to a peak of 5.1905 on Tuesday. Mark/franc rose more than a centime, but that was only a fraction of the dollar move.

Citing an undervalued dollar as exaggerating "intolerable" levels of unemployment, Giscard called for the government to announce its intention to fix the future euro rate at seven francs to one euro, equivalent to 5.50 francs per dollar.
Gaullist National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin said later that Giscard's analysis was "impeccable."
On Tuesday, Bank of France monetary policy council memember Paul Marchelli said it would be a mistake to start EMU with a euro that was too strong against the dollar.
"We are seeing the start of the big debate on what the dollar-euro parity will be," said Marchelli. "The discussion is only just beginning."
For currency strategists, however, the debate has two potential twists, which are both bullish for dollar/franc.
If Germany remains silent about French calls for an explicitly weaker euro against the dollar then, dollar/mark will rise and support a long dollar/Paris position, they said.

But if the Germans publicly balk at the idea of a weaker euro against the dollar, a rise in internal French pressure to weaken the franc before monetary union will lead to a weaker franc against both the mark and the dollar, regardless of the impact on dollar/mark.
The problem then, is how French policymakers would coax the dollar higher against the franc without destabilisiing it against the mark and risking monetary union.

"Europe in general, and France in particular, have had a chronic disposition toward a stronger dollar for years and have never been prepared to do anything concrete about it," said Adrian Schmidt, economist at Chase Investment Bank.

However, Schmidt said the rise of about 24 billion dollars in European central bank foreign exchange reserves in the first half of 1996 may be an indication of more resolve in buoying the dollar/Europe exchange rate, albeit in a covert fashion.
"There is still occasional talk of European central bank buying of dollars on dips, and it would not be unreasonable to expect some covert back-up on any serious push lower."
Nevertheless, stabilising the dollar and pushing it higher are two different things and the latter would almost certainly need some help from either U.S. or German authorities.
Few analysts currently see any signs they will sanction any dollar revaluation against Europe in the region of the 10-to-20 percent being touted in Paris.
"Gearing monetary policy to the euro's exchange rate against other currencies...is not a viable option," Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler said Wednesday.
